       Seven observations about weighted pseudorandom generators
                                   Dean Doron*                  Oded Goldreich

                                                    June 4, 2026


                                                       Abstract
           Weighted pseudorandom generators (wPRGs) were suggested by Braverman, Cohen, and
        Garg (STOC, 2018) as a relaxation of pseudorandom generator (PRG) used for derandomization.
        We present proofs of several observations regarding wPRGs, where some of these observations
        are well known.


Preface
In the context of “derandomization-oriented” pseudorandom generators, the verdict of a randomized
decision procedure D is emulated by a deterministic algorithm that invokes a “pseudorandom
generator” on all possible seeds, and rules according to the average value of D on the corresponding
pseudorandom outcomes. When using this strategy for derandomizing a randomized-time (resp.,
randomized-space) complexity class it is reasonable to allow the generator, called a “canonical
derandomizer” in [5, Sec. 8.3], to run in exponential-time (resp., linear-space).
    As observed by Braverman, Cohen, and Garg [1], in the context of using this derandomization
strategy, using a weighted average (rather than a standard (unweighted) average) is just as good.
Furthermore, it seems that this relaxation is beneficial [8, 2, 3], provided that one also uses negative
weights. In contrast, it is known that non-negative weights give no benefit.
    In this memo, we present a proof of the foregoing folklore as well as present a few other obser-
vations about wPRGs.


Preliminaries
A weighted pseudorandom generator (wPRG), denoted (G, ω), is obtained by augmenting a standard
pseudorandom generator (PRG) G : {0, 1}k → {0, 1}n , where k < n, with a weight function
ω : {0, 1}k → R. We say that a wPRG (G, ω) fools (or ϵ-fools) the distinguisher D if

                              Es∈{0,1}k [ω(s) · D(G(s))] = Eu∈{0,1}n [D(u)] ± ϵ.                            (1)
In particular, if (G, ω) fools (i.e., ϵ-fools) a class of distinguishers that contains the all-1 function,
then Es [ω(s)] ≈ 1 (i.e., Es [ω(s)] = 1 ± ϵ). Actually, recalling that wPRGs are used for derandom-
ization and so scanning all seeds is feasible, we may assume (w.l.o.g.) that the average weight is
exactly 1 (because we can compute ν ← Es [ω(s)] and normalize the original weights by ν).

    In general, when making “w.l.o.g assertions” about wPRGs, we allow for (1) increasing the
seed length (i.e., k) by a constant factor, (2) increasing the deviation (i.e., ϵ) by raising it to a
(positive) constant power, (3) increasing the space complexity (of computing the wPRG) by an
additive amount that is linear in the seed-length, and (4) increasing the time complexity by a
factor that is exponential in the seed-length. We shall also assume that ϵ ≥ 2−k , and that ϵ is at
most a sufficiently small constant.
    In the context of derandomization, the standard definition of a distinguisher is that it is a
function (computable within some complexity class) that outputs a verdict in {0, 1}. In other
contexts, randomized processes with Boolean output may also be considered, and when considering
their expected value one gets a function that ranges over [0, 1]. Since all observations hold also for
the latter case, we define a class of distinguishers as a set of functions from strings to [0, 1]. (We
note that some of the observations hold also for arbitrary functions from strings to R.)1


Observations
All observations are quite oblivious of the class of distinguishers, with the exception that some of
them require this class to contain the all-1 function. We first recall the observation made in the
previous section.

Observation 1 (the average weight approximately equals 1): Suppose that (G, ω) is a wPRG that
ϵ-fools a class of distinguishers D that contains the all-1 function. Then, Es∈{0,1}k [ω(s)] = 1 ± ϵ.

The following observation is well-known (at least to experts).

Observation 2 (non-negative weights are useless): Let ω : {0, 1}k → R+ (i.e., ω(s) ≥ 0 for every
s) and suppose that (G, ω) fools a class of distinguishers D that contains the all-1 function. Then,
D can be fooled by a standard PRG of the same complexity.

Observation 3 (extremely bounded weights are useless): Suppose that ω : {0, 1}k → R is upper-
bounded by 1 (i.e., ω(s) ≤ 1 for every s) and suppose that (G, ω) fools a class of distinguishers D
that contains the all-1 function. Then, D can be fooled by a standard PRG of the same complexity.
Specifically, if the wPRG ϵ-fools D, then the standard PRG 2ϵ-fools D.

This observation is implicit in the proof of [3, Lem. 5.6], which is reproduced next.2
Proof: On the one hand, using ω(s) ≤ 1 for every s, we have, for every D ∈ D

                                     Es [D(G(s))] ≥ Es [ω(s) · D(G(s))]
                                                      ≥ Eu [D(u)] − ϵ.

On the other hand, using 1 − ω(s) ≥ 0, for every D ∈ D, we have

                     Es [D(G(s))] = Es [ω(s) · D(G(s))] + Es [(1 − ω(s)) · D(G(s))]

standard PRG G 2ϵ-fools D.

B(k) ∈ [1, exp(O(k))] it holds that ω : {0, 1}k → [−B(k), +B(k)] and suppose that (G, ω) fools a

The complexity of the weights. In the context of “derandomization-oriented” pseudorandom
generators, one typically uses PRGs whose complexity exceeds the complexity of the distinguishers.
A natural question is whether this is needed also for the weighting function of a wPRG. A partial
affirmative answer is provided next.

Observation 6 (low complexity weights are useless): Suppose that (G, ω) ϵ-fools a class of distin-
guishers D that contains the all-1 function and that the mapping G(s) 7→ ω(s) is computable in D,
which indeed implies that ω(s) = ω(s′ ) if G(s) = G(s′ ). Then, D can be O(ϵ)-fooled by a standard
PRG of the same complexity. Moreover, the conclusion holds also if we only require the sign of the
weight to be computable in D.

Sufficiently good approximation
Bearing in mind that wPRGs are used for derandomization of algorithms that may be made to
have small error probability (by repetitions), it suffices to distinguish between a value close to 1
and a value close to 0. In that context, sufficiently bounded weights can be eliminated as shown
next.

that can be computed in linear space (e.g., [4]). Then, the new PRG is given by G′ (s, r) = (s, r, G(EXT(s, r)). (The
transformation applies also to wPRGs; however, it may not preserve the complexity of computing the weights.)

Open problems
While Observation 6 refers to the complexity of the weights, it actually considers the complexity
of the mapping G(s) 7→ ω(s). Indeed, it is more natural to consider the complexity of the mapping
s 7→ ω(s).


                                                     6
Open Problem 1 (easily computable weights): Suppose that (G, ω) fools a class of distinguishers
D and that ω is computable in D. Is it the case that D can be fooled by a standard PRG of the
same complexity? If not, then are there additional conditions that yield an affirmative answer?

Similarly, while Observations 3 and 7 refer to bounded weights, they refer to very restricted cases.

Open Problem 2 (bounded weights, revisited): Suppose that for some constant B ≥ 1 it holds
that ω : {0, 1}k → [−B, +B] and that (G, ω) fools a class of distinguishers D. Is it the case that D
can be fooled by a standard PRG of the same complexity? If not, then are there additional conditions
that yield an affirmative answer?

Of course, affirmative answers will beg the question of extending the result to adequately bounded
functions B : N → N.
